newsitem.title: USA: Rise in US prices sparked Brazil soy sale-US trade.
newsitem.headline: Rise in US prices sparked Brazil soy sale-US trade.

text.p: The sale by Glencore Brazil of 45,000 tonnes of Brazilian soybeans to a U.S. firm appeared to make economic sense following the run-up in CBOT futures to an 8-1/2-year high Monday, some U.S. export sources said.
Sources said Brazilian soybeans could be shipped to New Orleans for around 25-1/2 cents over May CBOT futures, compared with about 24 cents for U.S. soybeans.
The higher quality of Brazilian soybeans made them effectively worth an additional 15 to 20 cents a bushel versus U.S. soybeans, one exporter said.
"The numbers are making sense. The political issue might be worth three or four cents a bushel but would it be worth 10, 15, 20 cents a bushel? Somehow I don't believe so," one U.S. exporter said.
An influx of Brazilian soybeans to the United States could anger U.S. farmers and prompt them to move their business away from firms involved in the importing, exporters said.
They were not surprised the move had been made by a "pure trading house" like Glencore which has few links to producers.
"Maybe a Cargill would have a problem because they buy a lot from farmers," an export source said.
"Prices are out of whack right now. The guys in Chicago went crazy so either we realign the prices or this is something we have to face," he said.
Some export sources, however, expressed doubts about the viability of the sale.

"It is close economically (to being worthwhile) but when you add the political ramifications on that I don't think you have enough profitability to compensate for the publicity you might have," one export source said.
The news helped spark a sharp decline in CBOT soybean futures with May closing off 27 cents at $8.28-1/2 a bushel.

"It looks as though something was booked. The question is whether this is the tip of the iceberg or a flash in the pan telling us we got a little ahead of ourselves here. I think probably it is the latter," said analyst Anne Frick of Prudential Securities.
She could not however rule out the possibility Brazilian soybeans might be imported on "a regular basis" over the next few months given the tightness of supplies in the U.S.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture currently estimates U.S. stocks at the end of the current season (August 31) at 140 million bushels, compared to 183 million a year earlier.
